IANATA (tax attorney), but the short answer is yes, but you might not be able to keep your job. So companies do try to treat "employees" as contractors sometimes, and that can work depending on the exact nature of the working relationship. Primarily, if the company provides the equipment (think capital -- like a factory where all this originated) and you provide the labor, they have to treat you as an employee. Which means they have to withhold taxes and you aren't getting any tax breaks. If you are providing the equipment (think, well, a contractor, as in someone who builds stuff) and the labor, and they just give you a job to do and pay you, they can pay you as a contractor. This has several consequences. One you might note quickly is that they no longer have any obligation or ability to pay for your health care. Secondly, the employer's portion of Social Security gets transferred to you, making this initially kind of a bad deal. However, if you incorporate yourself you can start writing off all your expenses. You can depreciate your tools/your truck; you can write off your haircuts and your uniform/suit. You end up getting taxed based on the nature of the corp that you setup. S-corps have been in the news recently. Those are convenient for tax purposes since they "pass through" profits as income. And yeah, you end up responsible for legal costs.

From people I've known, incorporating yourself is a PITA that can be quite lucrative. Again, depending on the nature of your job, that might not be an option. I mean, you might have to quit as an employee and go seek contracts.
